findings.text: The spec says twice that nothing reads `latest` until piece 3 (Non-Goals; Risks "`latest` may lag"), and the code agrees: `compose.yml:6` pins `${WIZARDINGCODE_MEM_VERSION}` and no file uses `:latest`. So the contract hold protects no reader in this piece, yet it adds a source-text parser of `src/team/contract.ts` that fails closed, `previousPlain`, `decideHold`, a third dispatch input, two summary outcomes, a manual-release path and a runbook section. A builder would ship and test a gate for a consumer that does not exist yet, and would freeze its rule before piece 3 has decided how a host follows `latest`. The simpler shape: this piece moves `latest` last and does nothing more; the hold is built in piece 3 next to its reader. D-2 is the author's decision, so the session should confirm it was made knowing that nothing reads `latest` today.
findings.reason: The author was asked this on 2026-11-12 with the fact stated in the question (nothing reads latest today; the compose file pins the version) and with 'in piece 3' as the recommended option, and chose to keep the rule in this piece, corrected, with a manual release of the hold; the spec records it under Alternatives ('The contract rule moved to piece 3. Not taken') and as D-2.

findings.scope: Design "`token.ts`: the token's state" and `token.yml` (Goal 6, AC-28, AC-31, plan steps 22, 26, 27, 32)
findings.text: GitHub already emails a personal access token's owner, fine-grained tokens included, before the token expires. The spec also admits that the header the check reads may be absent ("expiry unknown … passes"). That leaves the weekly workflow, `door.ts`, the second environment check and `--fail-under` largely repeating a notice the platform already sends, on a signal that may not exist. A builder would maintain a second scheduled workflow, which GitHub also disables after 60 days without activity (the runbook's own limit), for little gain over the platform's email plus the warning on the release run. The simpler shape: keep `token.ts` as the first step of `tap` and `marketplace`, which gives a named failure and the under-30-days warning; drop `token.yml` and `door.ts`, or state why the platform's email does not satisfy Goal 6.
findings.reason: The author decided on 2026-11-12 (D-3) to remove the weekly check: token.yml and door.ts go; token.ts stays as the first step of tap and marketplace (a named failure, a warning under 30 days); Goal 6 is reworded to what that delivers, with GitHub's expiry email and the noted date as the advance notice.

findings.text: Three hand-written implementations of full semver precedence, one of them in awk, cover cases this project never produces: `0.9.0-aaa`, `0.9.0-1` against `0.9.0-rc`, and alphanumeric order by code unit. Refusal 2's tag pattern could narrow pre-releases to `-rc.<n>`. Then the JS and shell `older()` need only compare the core and an integer rc number, and `Bun.semver.order` stays the one full implementation on the TypeScript side.
findings.reason: The order stays semver's: the plugins' existing test stages a '-aaa' pre-release, binaries already in the field may carry any pre-release, and a rule narrower than Bun.semver.order on the TypeScript side would make the three texts disagree again.

findings.text: The edit is a bespoke text scanner that matches braces outside strings so that every other byte stays the same. A shorter path gives the same guarantee: refuse a file where `JSON.stringify(JSON.parse(text), null, 2) + "\n"` does not equal the text, otherwise parse, set the two fields and stringify again. The fixtures copied from the marketplace already show whether the files round-trip.
findings.reason: The agents' manifest does not round-trip through JSON.stringify (it holds inline objects such as { "displayName": "WizardingCode" } on one line), so a parse-and-stringify would rewrite bytes this item must leave alone, or refuse the file on every release.

findings.text: The spec's Design names helper functions and their file locations (`summaryLine(target, outcome)` in `lib.ts`, `olderThan(have, wanted)`, `OLDER_JS`) and dated npm facts ("what npm 11.19.0 answered … on 2026-11-12"). That is plan-level detail. The spec needs the fixed texts table and the contract "a registry error is never read as not published"; the plan already carries the names.
findings.reason: The names stay in the spec where a criterion cites them (olderThan, OLDER_JS, summaryLine): the criteria are read against the spec. The dated npm fact stays as provenance of the rule it backs.

findings.text: A fourth command file, with a checkout and a Bun setup, exists only to print one summary line. `plan` already writes the lines of the targets it skips. It could also emit the `latest` line as an output for the job to echo through `env:`, or `latest` could run an existing command with a flag, so no new file is needed.
findings.reason: scripts/release/summary.ts is dropped: plan computes the latest job's line (moved, would move, moved by hand) as the output latest_line, and the latest job appends it to the summary through env.

findings.text: The "highest version" rule is computed over all of the repository's `v*` tags, not only tags whose commit is on `main`. So the J-8 attacker's `v99.0.0` (refused by refusal 4) stays in the tag list, and from then on refusal 6 refuses every real release (`v0.9.0` is not the highest plain tag) until someone notices and deletes the tag. The same unfiltered list picks the "previous plain release" for the hold. Anyone who can push a branch can stop distribution with one tag push. A builder following the text will filter the wrong list. The spec also does not say how a `v*` tag that fails the refusal-2 regex is ordered or skipped.
findings.reason: The tag list the rules read becomes the v* tags merged into main that are version tags (git tag --merged origin/main --list 'v*', filtered by the tag pattern): a tag on a branch commit, or one that is not a version, is counted by neither the highest-tag rule nor the previous plain release. With D-4 the ruleset on v* tags is mandatory, so such a tag cannot be created by a non-admin either.

findings.text: "Nothing else in the repository moves `latest` once `docker` stops pushing it" is false. A tag pushed on any commit runs that commit's own `release.yml`, whose token has `packages: write`. An older commit, or a branch commit, can still carry the `docker` job that tags `latest`. Separately, a branch's own `distribute.yml` dispatched from that branch can have a job with no environment and `packages: write` that retags `latest` to any image. findings.scope: The door, second bullet / J-8 / refusal 4
findings.text: The ancestor check is called the second barrier, but it only stops tags on branch commits. Without the `v*` ruleset (J-8's premise), anyone with write access can put `v99.0.0` on any old commit of `main` that carries `distribute.yml`. Refusals 4 and 5 then pass. Contents write lets them create the GitHub release by hand with six assets of their choosing, so refusals 7 and 8 pass too. They then dispatch `distribute.yml` from `main`. `npm` stops at the version check, but `tap` and `marketplace` need only `plan`, so they run in parallel and write anyway. The tap gets a formula whose URLs and checksums point at the attacker's binaries. The `v99.0.0` tag also blocks every later real release through refusal 6, so J-8's "a later real v0.9.0 is still distributed" is false in this case. `plan` never checks that the tag's version equals `package.json` at the tag's commit, and never checks that the release was created by `release.yml` and not by a person. A builder would treat the ancestor check as a real second barrier when it is not.
findings.reason: plan gains a refusal: the tag's version differs from package.json at the tag's commit (so a v99.0.0 put on an old commit of main is refused), and J-8 and the second-barrier sentence are corrected to what the checks give: they stop a tag on a branch commit and a tag whose version is not its tree's; a release made by hand on a correctly versioned commit of main, and a stray tag blocking later releases, are closed by the mandatory ruleset on v* tags (D-4), which Risks says.

findings.scope: The writers of `<data dir>/bin`, `wizardingcode-mem install` / AC-43
findings.text: When a newer binary is kept, `install` still goes on in the older running binary. That binary opens the store: `src/install/takeover.ts:48`, `history-offer.ts:97` and `semantic-offer.ts:87` all call `openDb`. If the newer binary has already migrated the schema, the older one throws `SchemaTooNewError` part way through `install`, after the hooks have been pointed at the staged binary. The spec says nothing about this case. It does not say whether `install` should hand off to the kept binary (as `install.sh` does), skip the store steps, or stop. A builder would ship an `install` that fails half-way in exactly the mixed-version situation this item is meant to fix.
findings.reason: When a newer binary is kept, install hands over to it: it prints the notice, runs the staged binary with the same arguments and returns its exit code, so no step of install runs in the older binary against a store the newer one may have migrated; the criterion and its test say so.

The first real dispatch is the real test, and a partial failure there is what leaves channels on different versions. The author would trust a check that cannot catch these failures.

A builder following the table would deliver summaries with missing targets on exactly the runs the author most needs to read.
